title: Prejudice in reverse; Hinton's side of eating apart
summary: Maxwell admits to overcompensating around Black musicians; Hinton explains why he stayed away from dinners for the white players' sake.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So all my favorites were that. And I'll tell you, it took me many years to get mad at a black guy, to be able to tell him to go screw himself, you know, because I was always sort of backing off. So in other words, I had a prejudice in reverse, there was a difference in my mind. It took me many years before I could behave the same to them as I did to anybody else. So in its own way, that was a prejudice.
Now, I don't know if I grew up with that or if I acquired it along the way but that doesn't matter. The point

is, I had it. Yeah, I'm sure. I've had that most of my life. I could remember working with guys like you, even as late as when we were down at Wister Hollow (PHONETIC), making all those dates. And of all my friends, all the guys that we were working with and yet, when you guys went to dinner, I always took off and would go some other place. Mainly because I didn't really know how to address myself to it and some places, I know, didn't want me in there. And they would perhaps be angry with you because you had brought me in there. And then rather than have it like that, I would go someplace else and meet you back there in the afternoon, for the dinner, for the next date. As late as that.
I'm ashamed that I never realized that. Because I have always been sensitive about that and sort of bend over backwards to be sure that doesn't happen.

Most guys were like that. I know my dearest friends like Buddy Laker and guys like that, we were together. But I would -- I can remember always (inaudible) I did because the inferiority was here and the inconvenience that that caused you. I didn't want anybody else to have to defend me. So I can understand your reverse prejudice.
